newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco opposition urges 'yes' vote in referendum.
newsitem.headline: Morocco opposition urges 'yes' vote in referendum.

text.p: After weeks of consultations, Morocca's main opposition parties called on Thursday on their supporters to vote "yes" in a September 13 referendum on constitutional reforms, a party spokesman said.
King Hassan announced last month the proposed constitutional amendment to split the existing 333-seat parliament into two chambers to strengthen regional representation in a new higher house.

"Despite their reserves on the content of the draft constitution, leaders of the Istiqlal party and Socialist Union of People's Forces (USFP) held separate meetings and decided to call on their militants to vote 'yes'," the spokesman said.
The Istiqlal and USFP, along with the former communist Progress and Socialism Party, have more than 120 seats in the current parliament.

But two left-wing groups, the Socialist Avant-Garde Democratic Party and the Democratic and Popular Action Organisation (OADP) called for their supporters to vote against the proposed constitutional reforms.
King Hassan, 67, earlier called on Moroccan people to vote in favour of the constitutional amendment.
He named the new chamber as Majlis al-Mustasharin (Consultative Chamber) but "with a decision-making power...and initiative to pass a vote of no confidence against the government."
The 108-article constitution aims at setting up a bicameral parliament and new electoral laws, the king said.
A series of laws over the role and structures of both chambers will be presented before parliament for a vote in the session starting in October.
The parliament is expected to be dissolved by the end of December to start the campaign for the general elections. The king gave no details of the number of deputies in the future parliament.
The draft constitution contains six new articles compared with the 1992 constitution but no changes were made in the chapter related to the monarch's strong powers.
Both polls will also take in the disputed Western Sahara provinces under Moroccan administration since 1976.
The desert territory, whose independence is sought by the Polisario Front, has a dozen deputies in the present parliament that was elected in 1993.
